title: Insulin Physiology and Acute Complications of Diabetes Mellitus

questions.q: Match the following insulin features — 1) Chain length 2) Receptor type 3) Receptor kinase 4) Pre-prohormone … A) 51 amino acids in two chains B) Tyrosine kinase receptor C) Insulin receptor substrate (IRS) D) Preproinsulin
questions.exp: Insulin has 51 amino acids in two chains; receptor is a tyrosine kinase; downstream signalling uses IRS proteins; the precursor is preproinsulin. (Book p927)

questions.q: A neonate has refractory hyperglycaemia with severe insulin resistance and elevated triglycerides. The most likely genetic defect involves the:
questions.exp: Severe insulin resistance with hyperglycaemia in a neonate is consistent with insulin-receptor mutations (Donohue or Rabson-Mendenhall). (Book p927)

questions.q: Assess insulin structure: I Insulin is composed of A and B chains linked by disulphide bridges. II C-peptide remains attached in mature insulin.
questions.exp: Insulin has A and B chains linked by disulphide bonds; C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin and is not part of mature insulin. (Book p927)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a step in insulin biosynthesis?
questions.exp: Insulin does not directly produce glucose; it lowers glucose by promoting uptake and inhibiting production. (Book p927)

questions.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose primarily by stimulating glucose uptake via ___ translocation.
questions.exp: GLUT4 translocation to the muscle and adipocyte membrane is insulin's main glucose-lowering step. (Book p927)

questions.q: Match the following stimulus — 1) Glucose 2) Amino acids (especially leucine) 3) Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) 4) Vagal stimulation … A) Most potent stimulus for insulin secretion B) Stimulus during protein-rich meals C) Augment glucose-stimulated secretion D) Cephalic-phase insulin release
questions.exp: Glucose is the most potent stimulus; amino acids (especially leucine) trigger protein-meal insulin; incretins augment glucose-stimulated secretion; vagal activity drives cephalic-phase release. (Book p927)

questions.q: A patient has postprandial hypoglycaemia after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. The most consistent mechanism is:
questions.exp: Roux-en-Y bypass causes rapid glucose delivery with exaggerated GLP-1 and insulin surges, producing late hypoglycaemia. (Book p927)

questions.q: Assess insulin secretion phases: I First phase peaks within minutes and lasts ~10 minutes. II Second phase is sustained and involves newly synthesised insulin.
questions.exp: First phase releases stored granules within minutes; second phase is sustained and involves newly synthesised insulin. (Book p927)

questions.q: Match the following ion channel / enzyme — 1) K-ATP channel 2) Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel 3) KIR6.2 subunit 4) SUR1 subunit … A) Closes on ATP rise B) Opens to trigger exocytosis C) Forms pore of K-ATP D) Sulfonylurea receptor
questions.exp: ATP closes K-ATP channels; depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels triggering exocytosis; KIR6.2 forms the pore and SUR1 binds sulfonylureas. (Book p927)

questions.q: A patient uses sulfonylurea and experiences hypoglycaemia. The mechanism is most consistent with:
opts: Closure of K-ATP channels on β-cells
questions.exp: Sulfonylureas bind SUR1, closing K-ATP channels, depolarising the β-cell and triggering insulin release. (Book p927)

questions.q: Insulin receptor signalling involves phosphorylation of ___ proteins.
questions.exp: IRS proteins are phosphorylated by the insulin-receptor tyrosine kinase, activating PI3K and downstream metabolic effects. (Book p927)

questions.q: Assess insulin effects: I Insulin suppresses lipolysis in adipocytes. II Insulin stimulates glycogenolysis in liver.
questions.exp: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and gluconeogenesis; it stimulates glycogen synthesis, not glycogenolysis. (Book p927)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: Match the following GLUT transporter to its tissue distribution — 1) GLUT1 2) GLUT2 3) GLUT3 4) GLUT4 … A) Brain, kidney, colon, placenta, RBC B) Liver, β-cells, gut, kidney C) Brain, kidney, placenta D) Skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, adipose
questions.exp: GLUT1 is in brain, kidney, colon, placenta, RBC; GLUT2 in liver, β-cells, gut, kidney; GLUT3 in brain, kidney, placenta; GLUT4 in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and adipose tissue. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: A patient on insulin has unexplained hypoglycaemia; C-peptide is undetectable. The most consistent interpretation is:
questions.exp: Undetectable C-peptide with hypoglycaemia indicates exogenous insulin (since C-peptide is cleaved from endogenous insulin in equimolar amounts). (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: Assess C-peptide: I It is cleaved from proinsulin. II C-peptide is elevated in exogenous insulin use.
questions.exp: C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin and is not elevated by exogenous insulin; it is high in insulinoma and sulfonylurea use. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a state with raised C-peptide?
questions.exp: Exogenous insulin suppresses C-peptide; the other states raise endogenous insulin (and therefore C-peptide). (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: GLUT2 is a bidirectional, low-affinity transporter present on pancreatic ___ cells.
questions.exp: GLUT2 on β-cells senses glucose and is part of the glucose-stimulated insulin secretion pathway. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: Match the following transporter to its ligand / property — 1) GLUT5 2) SGLT1 3) SGLT2 4) GLUT4 … A) Fructose transporter B) Sodium-glucose cotransporter in gut C) Sodium-glucose cotransporter in PCT D) Insulin-stimulated glucose transporter
questions.exp: GLUT5 transports fructose; SGLT1 is in gut; SGLT2 in PCT; GLUT4 is insulin-stimulated. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: A patient is on empagliflozin. The mechanism is most consistent with:
opts: SGLT2 inhibition in proximal convoluted tubule
questions.exp: Empagliflozin inhibits SGLT2 in the PCT, reducing glucose reabsorption and producing glycosuria. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: Assess incretins: I GLP-1 is secreted by L-cells in the ileum and colon. II GIP is secreted by K-cells in the jejunum.
questions.exp: GLP-1 is secreted by ileal/colonic L-cells; GIP is secreted by K-cells in the jejunum. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: Match the following GLP-1 / GIP feature — 1) Half-life of GLP-1 2) Half-life of GIP 3) Action of GLP-1 4) Action of GIP … A) 1–2 minutes B) 5–7 minutes C) Glucose-dependent insulin release, satiety D) Insulin release in response to fat
questions.exp: GLP-1 has half-life 1–2 min; GIP has 5–7 min; GLP-1 produces glucose-dependent insulin release and satiety; GIP releases insulin in response to fat. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: A patient on semaglutide oral achieves HbA1c reduction with weight loss. The mechanism is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist with weight-loss and HbA1c-reducing effects; DPP-4 inhibitors raise endogenous GLP-1 but cause less weight loss. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: C-peptide is high in endogenous hyperinsulinaemia (insulinoma) and low in ___ insulin use.
questions.exp: Exogenous insulin suppresses C-peptide, whereas insulinoma and sulfonylureas elevate it. (Book p928)

questions.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
questions.q: Assess the table: I Type 1 diabetes has undetectable C-peptide. II Type 2 diabetes has raised C-peptide early in disease.
questions.exp: Type 1 has low/undetectable C-peptide; Type 2 has raised C-peptide early due to insulin resistance, then falls as β-cell function declines. (Book p928)

questions.q: Match the following GLP-1 agonist to its feature — 1) Exenatide 2) Liraglutide 3) Semaglutide 4) Tirzepatide … A) Twice daily injection B) Once daily injection C) Once weekly oral / injectable D) Dual GLP-1/GIP agonist
questions.exp: Exenatide is twice daily; liraglutide is once daily; semaglutide is once weekly oral or injectable; tirzepatide is a dual GLP-1/GIP agonist. (Book p929)

questions.q: A patient on a GLP-1 agonist develops acute abdominal pain with elevated lipase. The most consistent drug class complication is:
questions.exp: GLP-1 agonists (especially exenatide) carry a class warning for acute pancreatitis. (Book p929)

questions.q: Assess GLP-1 agonists: I They cause glucose-dependent insulin secretion. II They promote glucagon release in hypoglycaemia.
questions.exp: GLP-1 agonists stimulate insulin and suppress glucagon in a glucose-dependent manner, limiting hypoglycaemia. (Book p929)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a non-GLP-1 injectable hypoglycaemic agent?
questions.exp: Tirzepatide is a dual GLP-1/GIP agonist; the others are basal insulin analogues. (Book p929)

questions.q: The dual incretin agonist tirzepatide combines GLP-1 agonism with ___ agonism.
questions.exp: Tirzepatide combines GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonism, producing greater HbA1c reduction and weight loss than GLP-1 agonists alone. (Book p929)

questions.q: Match the following GLP-1 agonist to its main clinical strength — 1) Liraglutide 2) Semaglutide 3) Exenatide LAR 4) Dulaglutide … A) Cardiovascular outcome trial benefit B) HbA1c and weight loss C) Once-weekly injectable D) Easy-to-use pen
questions.exp: Liraglutide has landmark cardiovascular outcome data; semaglutide produces the largest HbA1c and weight loss; exenatide LAR is once-weekly; dulaglutide offers a simple weekly pen. (Book p929)

questions.q: A patient with T2DM and CKD benefits from a GLP-1 agonist. Which renal protective mechanism is most cited?
opts: Improvement in albuminuria and slowing of GFR decline
questions.exp: GLP-1 agonists reduce albuminuria and slow GFR decline via metabolic and haemodynamic effects. (Book p929)

questions.q: Assess GLP-1 adverse effects: I Nausea is common, especially with dose escalation. II GLP-1 agonists are contraindicated in pregnancy.
questions.exp: Nausea is common during titration; GLP-1 agonists are not approved in pregnancy and are stopped before conception. (Book p929)

questions.q: Match the following GLP-1 / GIP property — 1) Source of exenatide 2) Source of liraglutide 3) Liraglutide modification 4) Semaglutide modification … A) Exendin-4 from Gila monster B) Modified GLP-1 analogue C) C16 fatty-acid side chain for albumin binding D) Similar acylation for half-life extension
questions.exp: Exenatide is derived from exendin-4 (Gila monster); liraglutide is a modified GLP-1 with a fatty acid side chain for albumin binding; semaglutide has similar acylation to extend half-life. (Book p929)

questions.q: A patient develops medullary thyroid carcinoma while on a GLP-1 agonist. The most consistent mechanism is:
questions.exp: GLP-1 receptor activation on thyroid C-cells produces calcitonin release and may contribute to C-cell hyperplasia in rodents. (Book p929)

questions.q: Tirzepatide's effect on weight is most consistent with ___ levels of weight loss in trials.
questions.exp: Tirzepatide produces greater weight loss than GLP-1 agonists alone, with some patients achieving >15% weight reduction. (Book p929)

questions.q: Assess GLP-1 / GIP cardiovascular outcome trials: I Liraglutide reduced MACE in high-risk patients. II Semaglutide showed cardiovascular benefit in the SUSTAIN-6 trial.
questions.exp: LEADER (liraglutide) and SUSTAIN-6 (semaglutide) both showed cardiovascular benefit in high-risk T2DM. (Book p929)

questions.q: Match the following DKA feature — 1) Trigger 2) Anion gap 3) Potassium 4) Plasma glucose … A) Infection, MI, missed insulin, pregnancy, cocaine B) Raised with positive ketones C) Total body depletion despite normal/raised serum K+ D) 250–600 mg/dL
questions.exp: Triggers include infection, MI, missed insulin, pregnancy and cocaine; AG is raised with positive ketones; total body K+ is depleted despite serum K+ often being normal/raised; plasma glucose is typically 250–600 mg/dL. (Book p930)

questions.q: A patient on insulin has a chest infection and develops Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain and plasma glucose 380 mg/dL with ketones. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, glucose 380 mg/dL with ketones fit DKA, often precipitated by infection. (Book p930)

questions.q: Assess DKA: I Insulin deficiency causes lipolysis and ketogenesis. II Hepatic ketogenesis is stimulated by glucagon excess.
questions.exp: Insulin deficiency and glucagon excess together drive lipolysis, FFA delivery to liver, and ketogenesis producing β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. (Book p930)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a feature more typical of HHS than DKA?
opts: Severe hyperglycaemia >600 mg/dL with profound dehydration
questions.exp: Positive serum ketones is a feature of DKA, not HHS; HHS has severe hyperglycaemia, high osmolarity and minimal ketosis. (Book p930)

questions.q: The dominant ketone body in DKA is ___.
questions.exp: β-hydroxybutyrate predominates in DKA; standard urine dipstick detects acetoacetate preferentially and may underestimate the true ketone load. (Book p930)

questions.q: Match the following DKA workup — 1) Glucose 2) Electrolytes 3) ABG 4) Serum osmolality … A) 250–600 mg/dL B) K+ depletion, Na+ artefact C) pH <7.3, HCO3 <15 D) 300–320 mOsm/kg
questions.exp: Glucose typically 250–600 mg/dL; electrolytes show K+ depletion and pseudohyponatraemia; ABG shows pH <7.3 and HCO3 <15; serum osmolarity 300–320 mOsm/kg. (Book p930)

questions.q: A DKA patient has serum Na+ 128 mEq/L and glucose 540 mg/dL. The corrected sodium is approximately:
questions.exp: Corrected Na+ ≈ measured Na+ + 1.6 × (glucose − 100)/100. With glucose 540, correction ≈ 128 + 7 ≈ 135 mEq/L. (Book p930)

questions.q: Assess potassium in DKA: I Initial serum K+ may be normal or high. II Insulin will further drop K+; replacement is needed.
questions.exp: Total body K+ is depleted even when initial serum K+ is normal/high; insulin therapy will lower K+ and replacement is required. (Book p930)

questions.q: Match the following DKA investigation to its expected finding — 1) Urine dipstick 2) β-hydroxybutyrate 3) Lactate 4) Anion gap … A) Ketones positive (acetoacetate) B) Elevated (best ketone) C) May be elevated if shock D) Raised (>10)
questions.exp: Urine dipstick detects acetoacetate; β-hydroxybutyrate is the predominant ketone; lactate may rise with shock; anion gap is raised >10. (Book p930)

questions.q: A patient with new T1DM has glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.18, HCO3 10 mEq/L and K+ 5.6 mEq/L. The first hour of management is most consistent with:
opts: IV fluids, hold insulin until K+ checked, monitor
questions.exp: Fluids and insulin are cornerstones; insulin should be withheld if K+ <3.3 until replacement; bicarbonate is not routine. (Book p930)

questions.q: The anion gap is calculated as Na+ − (Cl− + ___).
questions.exp: AG = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−); the alternative including K+ is seldom used clinically. (Book p930)

questions.q: Assess DKA triggers: I New-onset T1DM can present with DKA. II Pregnancy predisposes to DKA.
questions.exp: New-onset T1DM commonly presents with DKA; pregnancy increases susceptibility because of hormonal changes. (Book p930)

questions.q: Match the following DKA management step — 1) Fluid 2) Insulin 3) Potassium 4) Dextrose … A) 0.9% saline, switch to 0.45% if hyperNa B) 0.1 U/kg regular IV bolus then 0.1 U/kg/h C) Add KCl once K+ <5.2 mEq/L D) Add when glucose <200 mg/dL to allow continued insulin
questions.exp: DKA fluids start with 0.9% saline; insulin is regular 0.1 U/kg bolus then 0.1 U/kg/h; KCl is added once K+ <5.2; dextrose is added when glucose <200 mg/dL. (Book p931)

questions.q: A DKA patient on insulin infusion has glucose 190 mg/dL, K+ 4.0 mEq/L, pH 7.22 and anion gap still raised. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Add dextrose to fluids and continue insulin
questions.exp: Once glucose <200 mg/dL but anion gap is still raised, add dextrose to allow continued insulin infusion to close the gap. (Book p931)

questions.q: Assess DKA fluids: I Total fluid deficit is typically 6–9 L. II The 3/3+3/9+3/12 rule (page mnemonic) structures replacement.
questions.exp: Total fluid deficit is 6–9 L; the page uses a 3/3+3/9+3/12 rule (or similar) to distribute replacement. (Book p931)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — an indication for stopping IV insulin in DKA?
opts: Glucose <70 mg/dL with no IV dextrose
Anion gap closure and bicarbonate >18 mEq/L with pH >7.3
questions.exp: Anion gap closure, bicarbonate >18 and pH >7.3 are criteria for resolution and transition to subcutaneous insulin; the others are not transition criteria. (Book p931)

questions.q: DKA protocols typically add KCl once serum K+ falls below ___ mEq/L.
questions.exp: KCl is added once K+ <5.2; if K+ <3.3, insulin should be held until replacement. (Book p931)

questions.q: Match the following HHS feature — 1) Typical age 2) Plasma osmolarity 3) Glucose 4) Prognosis … A) Older T2DM patient B) 320–380 mOsm/kg C) >600 mg/dL D) Worse than DKA
questions.exp: HHS occurs in older T2DM, osm 320–380, glucose >600 mg/dL and carries worse prognosis than DKA. (Book p931)

questions.q: An 80-year-old with T2DM has glucose 980 mg/dL, plasma osm 360 mOsm/kg, pH 7.38 and minimal ketones. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Severe hyperglycaemia, high osmolarity, near-normal pH and minimal ketones fit HHS. (Book p931)

questions.q: Assess HHS fluid management: I 0.45% saline is often used after initial 0.9% saline. II HHS fluid deficit averages around 12 L.
questions.exp: Initial 0.9% saline, often followed by 0.45% saline as Na+ normalises; HHS fluid deficit averages around 12 L. (Book p931)

questions.q: Match the following DKA-vs-HHS lab — 1) Glucose 2) Osmolarity 3) Ketones 4) Anion gap … A) 350–400 vs >800 mg/dL B) 300–320 vs 320–380 mOsm/kg C) +++ vs ± D) ↑ vs N/↓
questions.exp: DKA: glucose 350–400, osm 300–320, ketones +++, AG raised. HHS: glucose >800, osm 320–380, ketones ±, AG normal or low. (Book p931)

questions.q: An SGLT2-inhibitor user has glucose 220 mg/dL with ketoacidosis. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycaemic DKA with glucose <250 mg/dL; recognition requires a high index of suspicion. (Book p931)

questions.q: Euglycaemic DKA is most commonly associated with ___ use.
questions.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors are the classical cause of euglycaemic DKA. (Book p931)

questions.q: Assess transition off IV insulin: I Subcutaneous insulin should overlap the IV infusion by 1–2 hours. II Bicarbonate correction is routine.
questions.exp: Overlap subcutaneous insulin with IV for 1–2 hours to prevent rebound ketoacidosis; bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidaemia (pH <6.9). (Book p931)

questions.q: Match the following insulin regimen — 1) Basal-bolus 2) Premixed 3) CSII (pump) 4) Twice-daily NPH … A) Long-acting basal + rapid bolus B) Fixed-ratio biphasic insulin C) Continuous subcutaneous infusion D) Conventional older regimen
questions.exp: Basal-bolus uses long-acting basal + rapid bolus; premixed is fixed-ratio; CSII is continuous infusion; twice-daily NPH is the older conventional regimen. (Book p932)

questions.q: A T1DM patient has fasting hyperglycaemia on NPH and normal pre-dinner glucose. The next step is:
opts: Switch to insulin glargine without evaluation
Review 3 a.m. glucose to distinguish dawn phenomenon from Somogyi
questions.exp: Differentiating dawn phenomenon (high 3 a.m. and fasting) from Somogyi (low 3 a.m., high fasting) requires a 3 a.m. glucose check before changing regimen. (Book p932)

questions.q: Assess dawn vs Somogyi: I Dawn phenomenon is treated by increasing night-time insulin. II Somogyi is treated by reducing night-time insulin.
questions.exp: Dawn phenomenon is treated by increasing basal insulin; Somogyi is treated by reducing night-time insulin to avoid nocturnal hypoglycaemia. (Book p932)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a long-acting basal insulin?
questions.exp: Insulin aspart is a rapid-acting analogue; the others are basal analogues. (Book p932)

questions.q: The page's '8-8-8 + 16 U' overlap regimen at diagnosis of T1DM combines morning split doses with evening ___.
questions.exp: An 8-8-8 short-acting insulin plus 16 U basal insulin covers meals and overnight; this split-mixed regimen allows individual titration. (Book p932)

questions.q: Match the following rapid-acting insulin analogue — 1) Lispro 2) Aspart 3) Glulisine … A) Rapid-acting B) Rapid-acting C) Rapid-acting
questions.exp: Lispro, aspart and glulisine are all rapid-acting analogues; differences are in excipients and onset (typically 5–15 min). (Book p932)

questions.q: A T1DM patient has recurrent nocturnal hypoglycaemia on NPH. The most appropriate change is:
opts: Switch to insulin detemir or glargine with dose titration
questions.exp: Recurrent nocturnal hypoglycaemia warrants switching from NPH to a flatter basal analogue such as detemir or glargine. (Book p932)

questions.q: Assess CGM: I CGM reduces hypoglycaemia in T1DM. II CGM is not indicated in T2DM.
questions.exp: CGM reduces hypoglycaemia in T1DM and increasingly is used in insulin-requiring T2DM as well. (Book p932)

questions.q: Match the following SMBG / CGM measure — 1) 6-point profile 2) Time in range 3) Glycaemic variability 4) GMI … A) Pre- and post-meal + bedtime B) Percentage 70–180 mg/dL C) Standard deviation / coefficient of variation D) Glucose management indicator from CGM
questions.exp: 6-point profile covers pre/post meals and bedtime; TIR is the percentage in 70–180 mg/dL; glycaemic variability uses SD or CV; GMI is the CGM-derived HbA1c estimate. (Book p932)

questions.q: A T2DM patient on basal insulin has TIR 80% with low glucose events. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Maintain current regimen and review CGM data
questions.exp: TIR 80% with no/low hypoglycaemia is generally considered good control; maintain and review. (Book p932)

questions.q: CGM-derived HbA1c estimate is called the ___.
questions.exp: GMI is the CGM-derived estimate of HbA1c; it is useful when laboratory HbA1c is unreliable. (Book p932)

questions.q: Assess adjustments: I +2 / −4 rule (printed) increases dose if above target by 2 units. II Insulin detemir can be dosed twice daily.
questions.exp: Page-print +2/−4 is a titration rule for above/below target; detemir is often twice daily because of slightly shorter duration than glargine. (Book p932)

units.title: Insulin: structure, secretion and signalling
units.sec: Insulin: structure, secretion and signalling · p927
units.guide: Insulin has 51 amino acids in A and B chains with disulphide bonds; the precursor is preproinsulin; receptor is a tyrosine kinase signalling via IRS. Glucose is the most potent stimulus; first and second phases of secretion reflect stored and newly made insulin.

units.title: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology
units.sec: GLUT transporters, C-peptide and incretin physiology · p928
units.guide: GLUT1/3/4 differ in tissue specificity; GLUT2 is the β-cell glucose sensor; GLUT4 is insulin-stimulated. C-peptide tracks endogenous insulin and helps separate insulinoma / sulfonylurea use from exogenous insulin. GLP-1 and GIP are incretins with different half-lives.

units.title: Incretin therapies and dual agonists
units.sec: Incretin therapies and dual agonists · p929
units.guide: GLP-1 agonists (exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide) and the dual GLP-1/GIP agonist tirzepatide reduce HbA1c with weight loss and cardiovascular benefit. Caution for pancreatitis and medullary thyroid disease.

units.title: DKA: pathophysiology, features, investigations
units.guide: DKA arises from insulin deficiency with glucagon excess driving lipolysis and ketogenesis. Triggers include infection, MI, missed insulin, pregnancy and cocaine. β-hydroxybutyrate predominates; urine dipstick detects acetoacetate.

units.title: DKA management, HHS, overlap
units.guide: DKA fluids start with 0.9% saline, regular insulin 0.1 U/kg bolus then 0.1 U/kg/h; add KCl once K+ <5.2 and dextrose when glucose <200 mg/dL. HHS has 12 L deficit, glucose >600 mg/dL and worse prognosis. SGLT2 inhibitors cause euglycaemic DKA.

units.title: Insulin regimens, dawn/Somogyi, CGM
units.guide: Basal-bolus, premixed, CSII and twice-daily NPH are the main regimens. Distinguish dawn phenomenon from Somogyi by checking 3 a.m. glucose. CGM reduces hypoglycaemia and provides TIR, variability and GMI metrics.
